div.head: Scene
div.stage: SCENE, the back room of an Apothecary's Shop: Hartshorn comes hastily out of the Shop, followed by Mrs. Hartshorn.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Harts.
sp.p: Sam Hortshorn, Sam Hartshorn! will you hear me, or will you not?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: I do hear you. Every body hears you. Did'nt you observe that deaf old fellow in the shop? I should have held him by the ears this week; you brought him to his hearing with a word. He's cur'd; I've lost a patient by you, Mrs. Hartshorn.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: How many have you gain'd by me, Mr. Apothecary? Whose business have you stept into? My husband's—poor dear man. Is there any thing in or about this house that I, weak woman as I was, did not bestow on you?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Yes, there is.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: What is there, I would know?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: The golden mortar over the door.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Aye, truly, it has been a golden mortar to you. Why then have you admitted a lodger into my house, without my leave; and why do you persist to keep her in it, without my liking?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Who is it that you do like?

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Not your Julia Clareville for one. I desire to have no more of her company: none of your Irish misses in my family. I know nothing of her, or her connections.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Then I'll tell you—Her father, Captain Edmund Clareville, was as brave a man as Ireland ever bred; and that is not saying a little for his courage. I was surgeon of his ship for six good years, and saw plenty of sharp service in the time. When his leg was shatter'd by a ball, I cut it off. It was like cutting my own heart out of my body; for he died under the knife, tho' it was as masterly an amputation as ever was perform'd. He was a friend and a father to me; and can you think Sam Hartshorn will desert the orphan daughter of his brave old Captain?—No, dammee, no; that scurvy practice never shall be mine.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: So much for your story: but there are more stories than your's; and some that don't tell to your Miss Julia's credit.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: That may depend upon who has the telling of them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: She is the talk of the whole place. All the idle fellows in Bath hover about the house, in hopes to spy her pretty face forsooth at the window.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Put your own face out, and disappoint them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: No people of fashion countenance her. None of them visit her.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: No, they visit the street. There they get colds and coughs,—and then I visit them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Aye, you visit! Where's the good of that? When my first husband was alive, he knew something. What do you know?—Ship-practice.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Well! that is a practice pretty much in credit. I am not asham'd of it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: You are asham'd of nothing, I acknowledge that—You are not asham'd of harbouring a Miss in my house, to be the gazing stock of the whole city. 'Tis making yourself a mountebank, a show-man. Therefore, as you took your Julia in, I desire you'll turn your Julia out.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: 'Sorry I can't oblige you.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Then, if you won't do it, I will.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Indeed you will not,

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Who'll prevent me?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Conscience—not your conscience, but mine.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Oh! what? You've a conscience; have you?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: A tolerably easy one. I have a wife also: I wish I could say as much for her.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: You have a memory too, I hope, and can recollect what you were when I demean'd myself to marry you—An understrapper in the shop, a whackum to my poor dear husband.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Take care I'm not a whackum to your poor dear husband's wife. Recollect I carry a cane not only for ornament but use.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Ah, you sea monster! do you threaten me?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: No, I hint it to you in time, because that's fair. I have a tolerable good temper while it lasts; but as it is just now a-going, you had best be gone first.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Oh, that you wou'd take your own physic, and give me a chance to outlive you!

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Come, come; that's pretty well. Take my own physic!—That's not much amiss. My dame has some with in her malice, and no want of malice in her wit.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Ah, now, my good Mr. Hartshorn, what have I done to displeasure your spouse, that she looks so black upon me all on a sudden?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Does she look black? Let her have a care she don't look black and blue too.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Ah, but look ye now, Mr. Hartshorn. You are my own kind friend, that is true; but that is no reason I should tarry in your house, when your spouse don't like my company. She is your wife; I am only your encumbrance.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Say no more about that; you are neither one nor the other, and she is both.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Well, but hear reason. You can't get rid of one, and you can of the other. I'll be looking out for another apartment.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Don't look out at all; but look to me for your protection. Your father's daughter shall not be the prey of libertines.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: What libertines want to make a prey of me?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Varnish, for one. He is a puppy, and a prig; I tell you that. I know him well. I wish you had never let him into the house.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: The house is not mine, neither is Mr. Varnish my visitor. Mrs. Hartshorn must receive what company she pleases.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Ah, Julia, you know why he visits Mrs. Hartshorn; therefore listen and attend to me, thou orphan relict of the best of friends! There is a man somewhere, upon sea or land, I know not which—I never saw him—to whom you should be kind; to whom you should be grateful.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Grateful! Explain yourself.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: A man your father form'd, protected, train'd to his profession; whom he lov'd, approv'd, confided in; and to whom (mark me, Julia) in his dying moments, (I was present at the time) amidst prayers and blessings (I held him up in his cot at that awful moment) Julia, your expiring father devoted you. That man is Sentamour, a gallant Captain in the British Navy.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Heaven protect him!

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Amen, with all my soul.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Why have I never seen him?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: A seaman's duty makes all else give way: His Country has had need of him.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Why have I never heard from him?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: I think you do hear from him.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Are you not regularly supplied with money for your accommodation and support?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Ah, now, my dear good Sir, inform me, if you can, who is that unknown friend to my necessities, whose bounties, so mysteriously convey'd, I never have been able yet to trace?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Nor have I; therefore I will not swear that Sentamour is the man; but I think I was not mistaken in my conjecture, when I said that you do hear from him. In short, Julia, I have a stump of the sea oak in me still; and when I hear of a generous action, which nobody fathers, I am apt to suspect that the heart which inspir'd it, will be found to beat under an anchor button: Therefore, again I say keep your heart for Sentamour, and beware of Varnish—

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Varnish, at your service—to that name I answer, worthy Mr. Hartshorn; and beg to know, if, when you warn this lady to beware of me, it is because you think me a notorious scoundrel. If that is your conception of me, only be pleas'd to say so, and give me an opportunity of correcting your mistake.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Sir! Mr. Varnish.—

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: I am all attention.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: When you enter a man's house without any introduction, and break in upon his private conversation without any ceremony, you must take your chance for what you hear, and seek your remedy as you see fit.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: And for efficacious remedies (I speak upon experience) Mr. Hartshorn the apothecary is outdone by no man. The golden mortar that adorns your door, is at once the symbol of your profession, and the safeguard of your person. I have frequently call'd you in, Mr. Hartshorn; I shall never call you out.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: If you never call again, I shall not break my heart.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: You see, Miss Clareville, what I submit to for your sake. Rescue me only from the humiliating necessity of visiting you in this filthy drug-shop, give me but one endearing proof of your confidence, and behold me at your feet.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: What proof do you require of me?

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Simply to assume a station worthy of yourself, an independent and respectable establishment, for which you shall be supplied with money to satisfy all possible demands.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: I am supplied to satisfy all reasonable demands; I have no ambition to enlarge them. I subsist upon the bounty of an unknown friend.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: But you can trace conjecture to that unknown friend?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Truly, Sir, I cannot; Mr. Hartshorn has his own ideas; but they seem to me so perfectly romantic, I can hardly credit them. They point at one far distant, whom I never saw.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: I am Mr. Hartshorn's most obedient humble servant; he has warn'd you against trusting me; I now caution you against believing him. Let him amuse himself with his idle conjectures, but don't permit him to mislead and puzzle you.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Ah, now, Mr. Varnish, be sincere. Could not you direct me better?

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: I profess nothing but to admire and serve you. I can enjoy the luxury of befriending innocence and beauty without the vanity and parade of publishing it.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: I understand you now most perfectly; and the nature of my obligations being such, you will give me leave to consider how the daughter of a noble and distinguished officer ought in honour to conduct herself—We must converse no longer.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: So! here's a turn—I have borrow'd a few favours of the unknown friend, and the fruit of my manœuvre is—We must converse no longer—She must deliberate, it seems. Be it so! She is a woman, and—The woman that deliberates is lost.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Friend Tom, friend Singleton, I want to have a little serious talk with you.

sp.speaker: Sing.
sp.p: Out with it! and as serious as you please.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Yes; I didn't come to this giggling place to be merry; I came to meditate. Prythee, Tom, didst ever meditate upon matrimony?

sp.speaker: Sing.
sp.p: Often; always. Therefore I never undertook it.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Right. Now I meditate upon it also, but can come to no conclusion.

sp.speaker: Sing.
sp.p: No, you will marry first, and come to your conclusion afterwards.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Would not that be very foolish?

sp.speaker: Sing.
Mand.
sp.p: But how if I do not approve of her, and yet am very much in love with her?—There is Louisa Davenant, for instance; I can't approve of her, you know; nobody can approve of her.

sp.speaker: Sing.
sp.p: A little volatile, perhaps—a little vain.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: No, she's not vain; there you are out; she's not vain; but she rallies without mercy, prattles without mitigation.

sp.speaker: Sing.
sp.p: Come, come, she prattles very pleasantly; has a great deal of wit, and an abundance of good humour.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Wit! not a grain, not an atom, as I am a living man; no wit—but affectation, vanity, as much as you can afford her.

sp.speaker: Sing.
sp.p: I thought you maintained she was not vain.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: That was because you maintained she was. I don't like to hear her found fault with.

sp.speaker: Sing.
sp.p: Well then, my good friend, we will say no more of her wit; you are not extravagantly witty yourself, so we will put that aside, and take for granted you admire her for her talents and accomplishments.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: She has no talents; never could be taught any thing. We are sister's children; I have known her from a child. She can't play a tune; no more music in her than a mile-stone; but then you know, Tom, I hate music.

sp.speaker: Sing.
sp.p: That's lucky. I hope you don't hate beauty too, for then I think you hardly cou'd like her.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: I like her because she professes so fixt an aversion to me, and seems to hold me in such sovereign contempt. That you know is so amusing, so animating before marriage, and so natural after, that we cannot fail to be good company.—'Sdeath! here she is!

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Cousin Mandeville, I have brought my work, and am come to sit with you.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Are you indeed?

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Your apartment is so shady and so sombre. We are burnt out of our lodgings on the hill.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Yes, you lodge upon the very top of the hill; that may be one reason why I lodge at the very bottom of it.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Oh you odious creature! Why don't you set chairs for us?

sp.speaker: Sing.
sp.p: None for me. I never make a third in such parties. I am for the pump-room.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: There! he's for the pump-room. Are you not for going there too? If you are, don't mind me.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Well, I don't mind you. But I am weary, and here I can rest both body and mind at the same time.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: And cou'dn't you have done that at home? I wonder, cousin Louisa, you don't sometimes try how comfortable it is to sit still and be quiet.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: I am trying it just now. When I want nothing else but to do nothing, and to think of nothing, you see I come to you; when I would seek pleasure and amusement, why then, cousin John, I go elsewhere.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Thank you; I am obliged to you. You are quiet here, I confess; perfectly still and quiet. You certainly are in no danger tête-à-tête with me.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: None in life. I bless the fates, cousin John, I can rub on as I am for some time to come yet.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Yes, yes, you can rub on very well as you are. You know you are not dying for me, and I am quite convinced I can live without you.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Very true. We can live tolerably well asunder: I am far from sure we could live so well together.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: No, no. Perfect happiness is not the lot of mortals. If we live single, you see we have cares; if we marry—

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Heavens! how they are multiplied! —Pick up my thread-paper. Don't you see I have dropt it?

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Yes, but don't drop it any more. I hate trouble.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Then you must never marry. That is nothing else but trouble without termination.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: And yet, Louisa, I cannot tell how it is, you seem to have fewer of those positives, that give trouble, and more of the negatives that prevent it, than anybody I am acquainted with.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Oh, yes; I have negatives in plenty, and for all occasions.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: I don't doubt it; and if you was called upon just now, you have one in readiness.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: At your service—one, and only one; for should you be importunate, and put me to repeat it, you know what two negatives make, and will interpret accordingly.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: There, there you drop something I am eager to lay hold of—

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Nothing is dropt. Here it is—a letter from your uncle.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: I receive no letters.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: What! not from your poor dear dying uncle? Not from Sir Mathew Moribund? Oh, fie.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Dying, do you say? What is the matter with him?

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Nothing is the matter with him; yet he can't last long; for he takes oceans of physic, has a whole host of doctors, drinks no wine, reads good books, and moralizes most inordinately.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Yes, yes, friend Raven, he is doing penance for his past excesses. Your master has been a hard goer, and is now pulling up at the end of his journey.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: He has had some amiable failings, sure enough; some elegant irregularities; but pray you now, Mr. Mandeville, be pleased to read his letter.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: “Dear Jack, It's all over with me. I have thrown off seven doctors and eleven apothecaries—”

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Seven and eleven—That's a nick.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: “I have now sent my rascal Raven to call in Hartshorn. There is but that one cast upon the dye for me.”

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Then he'll throw crabs, and there's an end of him.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: “I have still some hopes in Hartshorn, not only because I hear a good report of his practice, but because his name is so comfortable.”

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: I wonder then he keeps his rascal Raven still about him.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: “I hear also that Hartshorn has the finest girl in Bath, a lodger in his house— but what of that? I have done with all such; they are evil spirits, imps of the old one. Come to me however, dear Jack, whilst it is yet in my power to call myself Your's,“Mathew Moribund.”Louisa, how do you feel about this letter? You and I are equally allied to the writer of it.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Take your hat, and go to him. That is all you have to do.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Any answer?

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: None.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Any further commands?

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Not any.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Adieu! The rascal Raven humbly takes his leave, and will forthwith go in search of the rascal apothecary; that being done, nothing will remain but to shut the doctor's book, and open an account with the undertaker.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Come, set out, and be off to your uncle.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Why in such haste? All this is nothing. A meer fit of the meagrims, the old bachelor's disease.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Then look well to yourself, and take care you don't inherit something more than his estate.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Nobody but yourself can save me; you only have the remedy.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Ah, Mandeville, my remedy might be worse than your disease.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Don't say so; don't be so provoking, I can counterfeit no longer. The secret must come out: I am in love with you to distraction.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: I know that very well; I see that very plainly, and pity you very sincerely.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Pity! What's that? Pity is not love.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: No, but it is one of the family. Now don't say another word, but go to your uncle.—Good bye!—A pleasant walk to you.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: There, now you are laughing at me. That is always your way. I don't like it, Louisa: I fairly tell you I don't like it. And (what is more) I don't love you half so well as I did; nay, I am not sure if I love you at all.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Yes, yes, you do. Let us part friends at least. Give me your hand.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: I can't tell whether I shall or not. I am extremely angry with you. However, there is my hand: my heart is with it. Ah, Louisa, Louisa! you are at once the idol of my soul, and the torment of my life. Adieu.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Farewel!—So! what's the matter with me now? Oh lud, Oh lud!—Thank heaven, the man is more than sand-blind, and not blest with intuition, or he would inevitably find me out.

div.head: ACT II.
div.stage: Hartshorn's House; the room as before.
Hartshorn enters; followed by his Shopman.

sp.speaker: Shopman.
sp.p: An ill-looking fellow in the shop wants to speak with you.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: I hope he is as ill as he looks to be. Send him in.

sp.speaker: Shopm.
sp.p: Oh, but, Sir,—Squire Varnish has order'd in his bill. You have lost a customer.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Let him go. The devil doctor him for an unclean whelp. I care not.

sp.speaker: Shopm.
sp.p: What! don't you care when your patients drop off?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: No: 'Tis the nature of 'em. My patients have a trick of dropping off. Send the ill-looking fellow in.
I suppose he will drop off next.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: So!

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Well! So—and so! What more?

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Is that your golden mortar over the shop door?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: That is my mortar.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: And the name underneath it,—Samuel Hartshorn,—is that your name?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Samuel Hartshorn is my name. Put apothecary, surgeon, and man-midwife to it, you have all that you can want of me.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: I want nothing of you as man-midwife. My master Sir Matthew Moribund is not breeding—Hold! don't let me quite say that— he breeds meagrims and maggots, begot upon him by blue-devils, who ride him night and day in the shapes of gallipots and glass phials, with halters of white paper round their necks; whereby they stand as thick in his bed-chamber, as the frogs did in Pharoah's.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Before you go any farther, is he alive?

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Alive! what a question is that?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: A very natural one, after your account of him. A very necessary one also; for, if he is not alive, I can be of no service to him.

sp.speaker: Rav.
Harts.
sp.p: Take notice I will come. I understand he has seen a pretty many physicians.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Yes, and swallow'd all the physic they prescrib'd for him.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: That is his fault, and not theirs. Has not your master been a remarkable free-liver?

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: A damnable one.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: And do his physicians allow him wine now?

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: The devil a drop.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Well, we shall see. Reach me that cane, if you please—I'll trouble you for my hat. Now tell Sir Matthew Moribund I will have the honour to attend upon him; and harkee. friend, walk leisurely home; take your time, The hills are steep, and you seem very feeble.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Yes, I am married.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: So am I.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: The worse luck our's. Good bye to you.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: 'Sdeath, if I don't fetch this Sir Moribund up with a wet sail, I have learnt my practice in a King's ship for nothing.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: O I forgot to ask you where the sexton lives. I take it for granted he's a friend of your's.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: A near neighbour. You'll find him at work in the church-yard close by. Suppose you let him take measure of you: it may save some time.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: It may, it may; I thank you for the hint.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: There's a death-watch. There's a memento mori for a poor hipt devil dying of the meagrims.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: One word before you go out, my good Mr. Hartshorn.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Let it be one word. I'm in great haste.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: You are wrong in your conjectures about Captain Sentamour. It is not he, but Mr. Varnish, that has administer'd to my necessities since my father's death.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: I don't believe a word of it.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: You won't believe a word of it. He has all but confess'd it.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: If he had quite confess'd it, if he had sworn it, I would'nt listen to him. Julia, it's a flam, a trap, a false pretence to ensnare you. There is no trust in his word, no honour in his heart.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Nay, but be candid, my good friend; be just.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: I am just; but I can't stay to talk with you; I expect a gentleman from London by this day's coach, who is an intimate of Captain Sentamour's; wait only his arrival, and all shall be made clear to you.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: He is obstinate against conviction. 'Tis in vain to talk to him.

div.stage: Scene changes to Sir Mathew Moribund's sick chamber. He is discovered sitting in his night-gown and cap. Nurse attending.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Nurse, wheel the chair a little onwards—Any message from my nephew Mandeville?

sp.speaker: Nurse.
sp.p: None, Sir Mathew.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Is Raven returned yet?

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Here am I.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: You've been a long time gone. You see I am still alive.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Are you indeed? I could'nt have believ'd it.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Rascal, you are always croaking.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Yes, I do that by instinct.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Have you seen my nephew John?

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Yes, and your niece, Louisa. I gave them your letter.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Did they read it?

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: With difficulty.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Much affected by it?

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Prodigiously.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: What answer?

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: They are coming to dine, and pass the evening with you.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: They are mad, and you're a fool. Will this apothecary with the fine name come? Will he draw his cork, and comfort me with a taste of his spirit?

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Yes, you'll have taste and smell too, when he draws his corks, never fear. Oh! here he is; this is the golden mortar.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Very hot—quite sultry. Bad weather for sick folks; not so for doctors.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Sit down, Sir; sit down, Mr. Hartshorn, and recollect yourself. Take your time to consider of my case, and enquire into symptoms.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: How do you do? That's the first enquiry. If well, that's the best symptom.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: What are you talking of? If I were well, I would not send for you.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: And if I were no worse than you are, I would n't send for anybody.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: You are beside yourself. I can't be worse.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Proud to hear it. Any change must be for the better.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Sir, you talk a very odd language to a patient you never visited before—Neither have you touch'd my pulse.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Gadso! I forgot that. Give me your hand.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Well! How do you find it?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Just as I expected—Can't find it at all. But never mind that; I'll soon conjure up a pulse. Is this fellow your butler?

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Yes—I am the butler.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: What is that to the purpose?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Is he a good hand at drawing a cork.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: I've been out of practice lately.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: How much physic have you taken?

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Oceans.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Perhaps you havn't taken enough.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Look at those phials.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Phials! What are they good for? I administer my doses in quarts—rare old Madeira; East India physic,—brought it home with me; drink a good deal of it myself. I'll send you some in; you must finish a whole bottle before you go to bed.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Are you in earnest? Nothing else?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: You want nothing else.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: What! Will you send me in no physic?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Plenty, if you'll promise not to take it. To be serious—Invite your friends, drink your wine, cheer your spirits, throw that old night-cap into the fire, and my physic out of the window—You'll be well to-morrow.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: You are a comforter indeed! I see you are no friend to physic.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: O yes, I am—a great friend to physic. Live by selling it—more than they do that swallow it. Adieu!

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Hold, hold! Don't run off in such a hurry. Touch my pulse once more.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Damn your pulse! Never think about it. Must be gone—Good day to you!

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Damn my pulse!

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Yes, damn your pulse. That goes for nothing, you know, for you have no pulse.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: 'Tis false: I have a pulse. Hope raises it; expectation quickens it. Give me your arm. Richard's himself again. No physic—a bottle of Madeira!

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Huzza! Hartshorn and the golden mortar for ever!

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Now, shipmate here we are in Bath, and in this street, at the golden mortar, dwells Hartshorn the apothecary, on whom I have a design, in which, friend Lindsay, you must assist me. So, be prepared.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: I hope I shall be always prepar'd to obey the commands of Captain Sentamour.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Spoke like a seaman, and a seaman's friend—I presume you notic'd the conversation of a communicative gentleman in the mail coach with us, who talk'd much about a certain Julia Clareville, whom he call'd the Beauty of Bath. He gave us a list of her admirers, but insinuated that a young man of fashion, a Mr. Varnish, was the favour'd lover. In that lady's fame and fortune I am most particularly interested.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: So indeed you seem'd to be.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Yes, Sir, Julia Clareville is the orphan daughter of a naval hero, who was a father to me, when I had neither parent nor friend on earth to help me. She is now as destitute and dependent as I was when her father protected and supported me. Can there be a duty more sacred than I owe to her, the relict of my benefactor! None; and the reflection how imperfectly I have fulfill'd it weighs heavy on my conscience: But my Country call'd me forth, call'd me to distant seas, detain'd me there, possess'd me wholly.—How cou'd I obey two calls, as wide asunder as the poles.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: You have fulfill'd the greater duty.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: And have not absolutely neglected the lesser. I have kept off indigence; she has not felt those wants, that money could supply. I wou'd now do more; I wou'd look into her heart, and convince myself how far the virtues of her father have been infus'd and foster'd in her bosom.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: You will have opportunity for that.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: 'Tis that I am contriving. She lodges with this very Mr. Hartshorn, to whom you are recommended as a partner in his house and business. Your person is unknown to him, and my project is to pass myself upon him in your character, for the purpose above mentioned— You smile, Lindsay. I can read your thoughts. You think my project is ridiculous.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Romantic perhaps; you cannot be ridiculous.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Hear me. I want your name for little else than as an introduction, and you know we hold it fair to reconnoitre under false colours, tho' not so to engage. Do you conceive me now, or shall I open myself farther?—I wou'd not approach her as Sentamour, because I wou'd make no claim upon her gratitude; I would not purchase an opinion from her by money, by worldly prudence, or even by filial duty and obedience to her father's wishes. If she prefers Varnish, and he honorably proposes, let her marry him: As Lindsay, I obstruct her not; as Sentamour she shall never know me. Now have I explain'd myself?

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Clearly. Your motives are, as they ever will be, noble and ingenuous. But Sentamour is a gallant captain, Lindsay an humble surgeon; how can you assume a character so opposite to your own?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: For the moment only. I don't mean to make up medicines, nor pass an examination with your intended partner. Hartshorn is a brother seaman, and a worthy fellow: if he finds me out, he will not betray me; and I have reason to know he will neither be offended with me for the imposition, nor with you for acquiescing in it. Does this content you?

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Perfectly.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Now then for the golden mortar— up anchor, and away!

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Miss Julia; Miss Julia Clareville, I say, answer me, in one word—will you, or will you not, see Mr. Varnish?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: In one word—no. Mr. Hartshorn has forbidden it, and I will not disobey him in his own house.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Then will you, Miss Julia, be so very obliging to me, and so very much your own friend, as to quit this house, and put yourself under Mr. Varnish's protection, by whose bounty you are maintain'd?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Madam, as to quitting this house, that shall be as you and Mr. Hartshorn may agree; but to your question, if I will put myself under Mr. Varnish's protection, I should suppose you hardly can expect an answer.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Allow me to say you are under very great obligations to Mr. Varnish.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: If I am under obligations to Mr. Varnish, it is for favors unsolicited on my part; and if in return for those favors he requires of me any sacrifice of character, or even of appearances that might create suspicion, his favors become insult, and his friendship a pretence.

sp.speaker: Shopm.
sp.p: A gentleman to wait upon you.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Tis' Mr. Varnish. I won't stay in the room, if he attempts to enter it—Ah!—

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Who are you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Lindsay, at your service. I believe I was expected by Mr. Hartshorn.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Oh, aye, Lindsay is the person's name, who was recommended to him as an assistant in the shop: sit down, sit down: he will presently be at home.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Pardon me, Madam; I cannot sit whilst you and this lady are standing.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Well, as you will for that; but I suppos'd you might be tired with jolting in the mail coach. I conclude that was your conveyance.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: You conclude very truly.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: I presume, by the information of your anchor-buttons, you are one of my husband's sort, a brother of the cockpit.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Exactly as you state it. I have serv'd in a ship of war; as Captain Sentamour's certificate will testify.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Aye, very well; you are to sleep in the house. I shall order you an apartment in the attic.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Mrs. Hartshorn is not extremely polisht. You will meet a more agreeable reception from her husband.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Have I the honour to be in company with Miss Clareville?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: I am that person.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Then I am to assure you of the most sincere respect and good wishes of Captain Sentamour.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Is he in good health?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: He is in perfect health.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: I am rejoic'd to hear it. Has he been fortunate at sea?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: He thinks himself extremely fortunate.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Of his gallant services we have had frequent accounts. Is he humane as well as brave? Do his people love him?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Such as he is, your father made him. His instructions are his guides, his example never out of his sight. The nearer he approaches to that model, the better officer and man he will approve himself. No one more reveres the memory of your father than Captain Sentamour.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: It does him credit. Gratitude becomes a hero. Did you know my father?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: I had that honour.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: When did you last see him, and where?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: The last time I saw him was in the evening before the fight off Copenhagen.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Alas, alas! In that action he received his fatal, fatal wound.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: It is a melancholy subject. Let me beg you to enquire no further.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: One question more—My father languished under his wound some days. Did Sentamour see him in that period?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Sentamour himself was wounded. He cou'd not leave his ship.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: So far he stands acquitted; but you said that Sentamour reveres my father's memory; if so, was it never told him what were the last words and wishes of his dying friend? Did he never recollect that there was a wretched orphan in existence, who, if Hartshorn reports truly, was bequeathed to his protection?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Certainly he well knew and recollected every thing as you state it.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: How hard then is the fate of that orphan now to discover, that she has been secretly supported by the bounty of one, who never knew her father, never saw him, and to whom she cannot say—“This is a tribute of gratitude to my departed father: This remuneration it does not humble me to accept of.”

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: And who is the person that has secretly convey'd to you those supplies, which Sentamour, as you conceive, so ingratefully neglected to provide?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: That person is Mr. Varnish.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Then I have been rightly inform'd that Mr. Varnish is the favour'd lover, the accepted proponent for the honour of your hand.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: No, Sir, I will never favour that man's proposal, who may have it to say he has purchas'd me with money, or supported me upon charity. I will sooner work for my bread than accept another farthing from Mr. Varnish.

sp.speaker: Shopm.
sp.p: A letter for you, Miss.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: “Lest, your last remittance should be expended, I beg leave to present you with the inclos'd.”—A bank bill for one hundred pounds. Again from Varnish! What can he mean? I will not keep it: I will not accept of it.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Hold, if you please! Hear reason, and be just. If this bounty comes from Mr. Varnish,—if every aid you have receiv'd since you lost your father has been bestow'd upon you by him, and nothing by Sentamour,—is it not fit and right you should give Mr. Varnish an opportunity of exhibiting his proofs, and allow Captain Sentamour a chance of accounting for appearances that are now so much against him? But we are interrupted—Put up your letter. We shall find a time—

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: My dear Mr. Lindsay, I rejoice to see you. Give me your hand. Welcome to Bath! Here we are—Just come from my round of visits; up hill and down hill. Sultry hot, quite a siroque; south-east wind; thunder in the air; sour the beer—bowel complaints— swell the sick list—work enough for both; holidays for neither of us.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Well, Mr. Hartshorn, mine has not been a life of ease. I am us'd to work.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: So much the better. Walk'd the hospitals—work'd in the cockpit—All credentials ready—Captain's certificate—good recommendations—nothing wanting.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Nothing of that sort, I flatter myself.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Pleas'd to find you tête-à-tête with my sweet Julia. Hope you have brought a pacquet of good news from Captain Sentamour— long to hear all about it. No time for questions now.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Nor any for answers it shou'd seem, Mr. Hartshorn. Your tongue runs too fast for the gentleman to put in a word.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Gadso! I forgot. Hav'nt introduc'd you to Mrs. Hartshorn—hav'nt made you known to my dear Dolly—
Fine woman; amiable creature; happy couple— perfect sample of true nuptial felicity.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Don't believe him, Mr. Lindsay. He gabbles without thought. There is no continuity, as my first husband us'd to say, in his discourse.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Pardon me, Madam, when I have such evidence of your powers to make him happy, why should not I believe that he is happy?

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Sam Hartshorn, a word with you! —Lindsay is a very fine fellow, but take my word for it he is no apothecary.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: No apothecary! Well, to be sure, you have had pretty good experience in apothecaries. I'll try him. Brother Doctor, I wish to have your judgement in the case of a certain Baronet I have just now visited—Patient hypochondriac, pulse feeble, small, compressible, hardly to be felt—nerves derang'd, solids relax'd, debility universal. What would you prescribe?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Oh the vengeance!—To a patient in that state, what wou'd I prescribe?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Yes; that's the question—What wou'd you administer?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Grog.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Grog! that's a dose for a boatswain. What wou'd you take yourself, or give to your friend?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Good old Madeira, if I cou'd get it.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Give me your hand! You've hit it; by the powers, you have hit it. Exactly my process with Sir Matthew Moribund.—Good old Madeira, if you cou'd get it—and you shall get it; so come along, for I have the best in England, and the ladies shall partake of it.

div.head: ACT III.
div.stage: Sir Mathew Moribund, Mandeville, Singleton, and Varnish. (An apartment in Sir Mathew's house.)

sp.speaker: Sir Math. Moribund.
sp.p: Now, gentlemen, learn by my example to cherish your genius with a generous glass, and keep off the foul fiend of melancholy.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: I protest, uncle, I shou'd hardly know you. It seems as if you had undergone a new creation.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Yes, Sir, a new creation brought about by an old recreation. Therefore look to yourself, John; don't dream of my estate, for I mean to outlive you, marry, and raise up heirs to the expiring breed of the Moribunds.

sp.speaker: Sing.
sp.p: And I, who am in no such haste to be married, will lie by for your widow, Sir Mathew.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: You'll find that a long waiting job, friend Singleton. As for you, Varnish, who have youth, fortune, pleasure, at your beck; make haste and enjoy them. I have heard wonders of your fair Hibernian. If you mean to snap her, be quick. I am thinking to throw out my hook.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Your hook is not yet baited, Sir, and mine is taken.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Are you quite sure of that?

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Are you quite sure of any thing? But unless you shou'd take a fancy to propose to her, I think I may be sure.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: You may chance upon a much more formidable rival in Captain Sentamour.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Captain Sentamour! Who is he?

sp.speaker: Sing.
sp.p: Nay, Varnish, don't ask that question. All the world knows him for a very brave and successful sea officer.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Well, Sir, let him succeed at sea, and let me triumph on the land. But since Mandeville thinks so favourably of his cause, and is so warm in his support of it, I confess that if I experience any change in the sentiments of Julia Clareville, I shall begin to apprehend I have more opponents than one to contend with.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Mr. Varnish will understand, that as I profess all possible esteem for Captain Sentamour, I am free to own that my good wishes will be evermore in concert with my good opinion; but as I am incapable of taking unfair measures in his, or any other man's, behalf, I must insist upon it that none such shall be imputed to me.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Mr. Mandeville, Sir, with all possible veneration for your principles, I have the honour to be your most obedient humble servant.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: John, John, why will you provoke a quarrel with that petulant young man?

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Judge me, gentlemen, am I in fault?

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: No, but the fellow's an egregious puppy.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Then I must wonder, uncle, why you live with him.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Whom must I live with, Sir, if not with puppies?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Just pop in to see how we are.—Oho! convalescent, come about again. That's well. Visit of form—glad there's no occasion for me.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Pardon me, my good friend, there is great occasion for you.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: How so! What's the matter? let me feel your pulse.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: No, no, just now I want to feel your's. In the first place, accept this for your excellent Madeira.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Won't take it. Put it down in the bill, Comforting cordial—Overcharg'd already. Won't be tip'd. Pestle and Mortar take no tips. Leave them for the doctors.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: But you have done me more good than all the doctors, therefore I don't see why you should be so disinterested.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Can't help it. Every man has his faults—Humble servant, Mr. Singleton—happy to see you look so well. A sign you are not my patient.

sp.speaker: Sing.
sp.p: 'Tis a sign I don't want a doctor, when I am not your patient. Is your expected partner Lindsay yet arrived?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Apropos! I have a note for you,
from Mr. Lindsay. I told him I should see you,
—Sir Mathew, I shall take my leave. You are now in right train; live generously but avoid excess, and you will be perfectly well.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: My dear, dear Golden Mortar, I must and will embrace you.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Have a care of my wig: Don't spoil my wig.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Henceforward be my oracle, my great Apollo!

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Yes, I serv'd some time in the Apollo. Good day to you!

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Uncle, I must take my leave of you.

div.stage: Louisa enters as he is going out.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Stay, Mandeville—Halt! for I have something to inform you of.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Ah, Lady-bird, can you find time to visit an old sick relation?

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: That you are old I deny; that you are sick I can't find out; that you are my relation is the only excuse I can make, for visiting the greatest rake upon record in all England.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Fie on you, slanderer; I am no rake. I am poor easy soul, that am sometimes led astray by my good nature to consort with rakes.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: For the purpose of reforming them.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Not altogether. Whilst they are sober, I say nothing; when they are tipsey, they won't hear me; if they are for gambling, what avails my preaching? And when they are for quarrelling, it's not safe to come between them.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: So much for your gentlemen rakes; but the ladies do none of these things, yet they sometimes want a little of your advice, I dare say.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: And some of them take my advice.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: In what particulars?

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: For instance—I have lengthen'd their waists, deepen'd their tuckers, cover'd their elbows, and burnt their wigs.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: You have burnt your fingers I believe, and nothing else.—Now, Mandeville, for you—I call'd, as you desir'd me, upon Julia Clareville, and was let in. She was greatly agitated, and had been in tears: She affected to say it was in consequence of her meeting with a gentleman, who knew her father, and had been talking to her about him; but I suspect that coxcomb Varnish is the cause of it.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: I rather suspect no coxcomb is the cause of it, but a very brave and honourable fellow, whom I have the happiness to call my friend, and for whom I should suppose it very natural for that young lady to conceive a tender sentiment.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: A tender sentiment—for the honour of plain English, tell me what you mean by a tender sentiment.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Love.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Thank you. I am further off than ever. Love is a puzzle I know nothing of.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: True, your acquaintance is with one of the family, called Pity.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Well, that's a tender sentiment, is it not?

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: A convenient one, so long as you can pass it off in exchange for love. Counters for current coin—Else I alone have demands enough upon you to break your bank.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Bring them in then. Make out your account against me. I warrant I can find effects to satisfy and escape the statute.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Harkye, John; when you carry in your account, take my Lord Archbishop's licence with it, and then let's see how she'll decide between them.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Oh, frightful! That would be a choice of difficulties truly. I am very much obliged to you, uncle Moribund, for the hint. If I copy your example, and neglect your precept, shan't you think I act at least as wisely as my adviser.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: No; for though I never married myself, I have a great deal to say in favour of the married state.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: More, I can believe, than if you had made trial of it.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: It matters little what I have made trial of—an idle, silly, dissipated blockhead as I have been, and now you see what I have brought myself to be—a wayward, whimsical, windmill-headed hypocondriac—this hour among the tombs, the next upon the house-top: —a fellow well to pass, as nature made me; as I made myself, intolerable, capricious as a spoil'd child, and pettish as a lady's lap-dog. Marry, marry, my dear children; marry, and club your wits to make each other happy; for, depend upon it, 'tis your only chance. An old bachelor is the most melancholy, poor devil in creation, and an old maid is—

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Never mind what she is, uncle; have pity upon the poor old maids, and say no more upon the subject.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: No, you must say no more upon the subject. Your chaise is at the door, and you must take a turn upon Lansdown, to brace your nerves, and whet your appetite.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Who says I must do that?

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: The Golden Mortar. He charged me to tell you so; he has taken your case into deep consideration, and has found out that air and exercise are absolutely necessary for you.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: A notable discovery truly.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Yes, and he charges nothing for it: he says, moreover, you must pay down all your subscriptions without loss of time, and present yourself at all balls, concerts, gardens, playhouses and public-places, for the good of your health, and benefit of those who conduct them.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Hold; not so fast. One prescription at a time. Louisa, will you trust yourself with me upon Landsdown, or has my lecture frighten'd you?

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Not at all; rather amus'd me; but I hear so many recommend matrimony to others, without venturing upon it themselves, that I begin to think those who know least, talk most, and those who know all, keep their own counsel and say nothing. Now, uncle, if you are ready I am with you. Mandeville will either stay at home and meditate, or take his horse and follow us.—Well! why don't you hand me to the carriage? Heaven help the man, he looks as dull as if he had come from Doctors Commons.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Ah, Louisa, Louisa; I am dull, not because I come from Doctors Commons, but because I can't find my way to it.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: O! Once get married, and you'll find your way to Doctors Commons, no doubt on't.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Come in, Lindsay! We shan't be interrupted. Hartshorn is not at home.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Well, Sir, how does your experiment succeed?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: I have just parted from Miss Clareville, and shou'd have put an end to my experiment, as you call it, by discovering myself to her, but that there is a secret smother'd in her heart, that puzzles me to guess at.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Do you suspect her of an attachment?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Certainly not to Varnish. He is entirely out of the question. But when I began to sound how her inclinations might be dispos'd towards Sentamour, and what reception I, as Lindsay, might encourage him to expect, her repugnance was so mark'd, and her agitation so evident, that I said no more upon the subject.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Permit me to observe, that I rather wonder you did not instantly discover yourself to her, state what you have been doing for her, and appeal to her gratitude for the preference that she owes you.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Lindsay, where have you serv'd? Not with me, I shou'd think, but on board some Guineaman, who trades for slaves, and, so he does but buy the body's use, cares little for the feelings of the soul. Have we so long been shipmates, William, and don't you know me better?

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: Sir, recollect you bade me call you Lindsay. If then I gave you sentiments that fit that humble character, it was because I did not think for you, but for myself.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Enough, enough! I wou'd not hurt you, Lindsay, for the world. Prepare yourself for Hartshorn. I shall give up Julia. I will be no man's second in her heart.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: It is not fit you shou'd. Is she as handsome as report gives out?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: When you ask that, I scarce know what to answer. I never found that beauty of itself was all-sufficient to enslave my heart: therefore I think it is not Julia's beauty, but something more impressive that has found so sudden and so deep a lodgement here.—But this is whining, lubber's language; so no more of it. Give me your hand. Don't think of what I said; let it pass off as my infirmity.

sp.speaker: Lind.
sp.p: O Sir, 'tis past, and left no other trace but of my faults, and your forgiveness of them.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Hark! some one's at the door! Be off at once. We shall soon meet again.

div.stage: (Exit Lindsay, and at the same time, Varnish enters to Sentamour.)

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Do you belong to this house, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: For the present I do. Mr. Hartshorn is not at home. What are your commands, Sir?

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: None for Mr. Hartshorn. My business is with Miss Clareville.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: You wish to speak with Miss Julia Clareville?

sp.speaker: Varn.
Sent.
sp.p: She is at home. What name must I announce you by?

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Varnish, at her service. I presume you have now your lesson.—Mr. Varnish desires to speak with Miss Julia Clareville; and be pleas'd to add to it—with her alone.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Here comes the lady.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: You will leave us.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Excuse me, Sir. In Mr. Hartshorn's house I am at home.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Mr. Varnish, I am fortunate in meeting you. I have some property of your's in my hand which as I have no present occasion for, I must beg you will permit me to return.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Madam, I don't know what you mean.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Ah now, don't deny it. You have taught me to believe I am so deeply indebted to you already, and money, Mr Varnish, is so suspicious a thing to pass between a fine, rich gentleman like you, and a poor destitute young woman like me, that, for my honor's sake, I must desire you in the first place to release me from this hundred pound bank bill; and in the next place let me know the extent of my obligations to you, and whether all or any of those secret supplies, which I regularly have received, and on which I have of late subsisted, were, as you led me to believe, actually furnish'd and supplied by you.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Miss Clareville, you will draw no such declaration from me, neither shall I make answer to any one particular, till you tell me who this gentleman, a perfect stranger to me, is, and by what right he is made a party in our conference.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Oh, Sir, that is soon done. The gentleman is Mr. Lindsay, and my very particular friend. Pray make no stranger of him; he knows the stiuation I am in, and the business we are upon.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Does he so? then he will receive no further information from me, he may assure himself; and as for the questions you have urg'd on me, you will do well to warn your prompter (for I'm persuaded you have a prompter) to take care I don't find him out; for if I shou'd—

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: What will you do to him?

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Treat him as his impertinence deserves. Let it be known to you, Sir, (since you are so curious to enquire) I will suffer no underhand intermeddlers to escape with impunity.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Indeed!

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Make yourself certain of that. I have declared myself the admirer of this lady; my pretensions cannot subject me to a refusal, my spirit will not bear an insult; my honour will not truckle to a rival. Therefore I let you know, (and you may govern yourself accordingly), no man living, least of all Captain Sentamour, shall venture to address Miss Clareville without accounting to me for his presumption.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Now, I should make no account of all those menaces, if I were worthy to address that lady.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: I admit your unworthiness, and you are indebted to it for your protection.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Hold, Sir! I bar all conclusions of that insulting sort. I may be, as I am, unworthy of Miss Clareville, and yet in no respect inferior to Mr. Varnish.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Who are you then, and what?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: The prompter, whom you threaten so severely. To spare you the trouble of seeking me out, I present myself to you.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Gentlemen, gentlemen! for heaven's sweet sake—

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Don't be alarmed, Madam; where you are present, the prompter is not seen.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Hear me, however; for I now speak to you on the part of Captain Sentamour, and require you to renounce all claim upon the gratitude of this young lady on account of those assum'd benefactions, not one doit of which came from you, but every one from Sentamour, as this deed of gift under his hand and seal will testify. There it is, Sir: the evidence is conclusive; and now what right have you to say, that no man living, least of all Captain Sentamour, shall address this lady without accounting to you for his presumption?

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: You will attend to the lady, Sir, who, I perceive, is under some degree of trepidation, for which, as far as it may have a reference to my sensibility as to what you have been saying, there is not the slightest occasion. The urbanity of your manners, the natural ease and familiar turn of your conversation, so forcibly impress me with the desire of knowing you better, that I shall seize the very earliest opportunity of inviting you to a renewal of our acquaintance, and of atoning to myself for the very short leave I am now constrain'd to take of you for a time, and of Miss Julia Clareville for ever.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: My dear Miss Clareville, what are you alarm'd at?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: At your danger. I am sure that man has mischief in his heart. Have no more to do with him. He is a terrible man.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Fear nothing; I have a way of dealing with terrible men, that is apt to make them very tame.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Why deal with him at all? 'Tis Captain Sentamour's affair, and he is absent.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: That he cannot be whilst I am present.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: True; you are his friend. I never saw him.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Never?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Never, to my knowledge.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Right! To your knowledge you have never seen him; but you'll receive this token by my hands.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Alas! alas! that I must live on gifts!—

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Miscal it not a gift: accept it as the legacy of your father, and consider Sentamour not as the bestower of a bounty, but the executor of a trust.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: May his benevolence be his reward? May Heaven shower down it's blessings on his head; may victory crown him, and protecting angels shield him from danger, wheresoe'er he goes! He has my prayers. I have nothing else to offer.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: He founds no claims upon you, imposes no restraints. Sentamour disdains the thought. Beauty like your's must needs attract admirers—If amongst these there is a favour'd and a happy lover—

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: If there is, Mr. Lindsay—if there is a luckless prepossession at my heart—

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: What then; what then?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: You are the last man living that shall know it.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Why so? What have I done? And why am I so pointedly excluded from your confidence?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Because—Dear me! because—Can't you guess the reason?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Indeed I cannot; at least I won't attempt it. Come, lovely, but mysterious tantalizer, tell me the man at once. I'll not betray you, and I pledge myself that Captain Sentamour shall not oppose your inclinations.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Now then I understand you—If, unfortunately for my repose, I may have fixt my affections otherwise than my father wish'd and recommended, you will pledge yourself for Captain Sentamour, that he shall not oppose them.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: I will.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Very good. So much for your friend —for yourself, I understand you will be my advocate with him for setting me at liberty; you, like Captain Sentamour, wish me to follow, where my inclinations would lead me, and without any remonstrance as to the object of my choice, wave all opposition to the freedom of it. Now, then, to your question, if there is a favour'd lover; I answer you at once, and peremptorily—There is not. Unknown as Captain Sentamour is by me, I have no remarks to make upon his motives for releasing me; but when you, whom I do know, can be so accommodating to my caprices, so ready to subscribe to my entire emancipation, I have only to thank you for the offer of your services, but am perfectly determin'd never to resort to them.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: There spoke the daughter of my gallant friend! This open display of her character cannot be mistaken. This interesting discovery I owe to my disguise. Now, if I lose her, I am of all most wretched.

div.head: ACT IV.

sp.speaker: Hartshorn.
sp.p: All this is well; all this is as it should be. Didn't I tell Lindsay we were the happiest couple in creation, and behold we are so! Good humour is a blessed thing; Good humour in a wife, my dear Dolly, is like gold leaf upon a pill; it does not alter the dose, but it makes it go down.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Very true, my dear Sam; very well compar'd. And when I see a smile upon my husband's face, as I do now, it seems to me like sunshine in a prison; it does not set me free, but it makes confinement bearable.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: You are right; it does all that; and I shall always smile whilst you look kind.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: 'Tis your own fault whenever I look otherwise.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Not always, Dolly.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Always, Mr. Hartshorn.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Come, come, lambkin, there are faults on both sides; but we'll not talk of faults: we will forget them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: But you do talk of faults; aye, and you commit so many, 'tis impossible to forget them.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: What faults have I committed just now? You have such a gentle way of bringing them to my recollection, I shall not be sorry to be told of them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: Look at your pretended partner Lindsay. What do you know of him? What does he know of his business? Have you ever examin'd him?—Not you. Are you sure he is what he pretends to be?—I much doubt it. Not one feature of the Apothecary can I see in his face, not one trace of the Hospital in his conversation and appearance.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: What then do you take him to be?

sp.speaker: Mrs. H.
sp.p: A very handsome fellow he certainly is; and without any compliment to his understanding, I take him to be very capable of outwitting you, and making off with your modest and immaculate Miss Julia. He is much more likely to be her partner than your's.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Say no more; I'll be up to him. Outwit me indeed! No, no, he'll not do that. —Mum! not another word.
Glad to see you, brother Doctor; glad to see you.—Dolly, my love, my life, we are upon business.

There! do you see that? A word, a look, a motion of my eye does it. Docile and obedient as a tame she bear. Now to business. I can assure you Mr. Lindsay, my expectations are rais'd very high by the terms in which Captain Sentamour and others have reported you to me. I flatter myself I shall not be disappointed.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: I am vain enough to think you will not.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Very good, very good. A little self-confidence in our way is not amiss—but to the point. My practice, Mr. Lindsay, you observe, comprises all the three branches, Surgery, Pharmacy, and the Obstetric Department:—In the two former well establish'd—full employment; in the latter, rising, growing, mending every day. Now there it is, brother Lindsay, there it is that I must look to you. When ladies cry out, it is but fit and right the young and able should attend the call, and take that duty from the old and feeble.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: With reason, Mr. Hartshorn, and they commonly do.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Good; very good again. Then you'll turn out, when Obadiah comes full tilt upon the coach-horse, and I'll keep snug the whilst.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Yes, I'll turn out if I hear him; but I am us'd to sleep in a ship. Noises don't easily waken me.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Not such noises perhaps as you are us'd to in a ship; but there are some that I am us'd to in this house will do it effectually, if others fail. You are handy enough no doubt in mixing up medicines, labelling phials, rolling up pills, construing prescriptions, weighing out drugs, and infusing them in their proper vehicles.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: O yes, all that is very easy.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: I am glad you find it so: I can't say I always do. Of chemicals and galenicals I need not speak diffusely.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: You need not speak a word about them. We'll agree to pass them over.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: We'll agree to no such thing. Pass them over indeed! I hope you understand their several powers, properties, and proportions; their compositions and decompositions, acids and alcalies, bracers and relaxers, quickeners and quieters, tonics and ante-tonics—

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Understand them all—What is an apothecary that does not?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: What is he?—Why, he is what many apothecaries are; what I have been, and what I am now—puzzled.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: I perceive it; instead of puzzling me, brother Hartshorn, you have puzzled yourself.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: D---ee, if I know whereabouts you are. Apothecary, or no apothecary—will you turn out, and take the round of the patients with me this afternoon?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: As I can be of no manner of service to you or to them, I had rather be excus'd.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: You had rather be excus'd! What the pestilence did you come here for?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: For an experiment.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: I'm oblig'd to you—You came for an experiment! Be so good to try the experiment of going away again.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Bear with me a little longer, and I will give you perfect satisfaction.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Give me the satisfaction of getting rid of you. If you will not go out and visit the patients, go out and visit where you like, only don't let me be favour'd with your company any longer.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: If I were Sentamour, wou'd you say this?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: No, d---,ee, no! To Sentamour my arms are open'd thus, as wide as I can stretch them—To Sentamour I say—Here is my heart, command it; it is your's!

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: I take you at your word, for I am Sentamour. Forgive me, my dear fellow. I was anxious to know the real character of Julia. I wish'd to see her under no restraint, and sound the secret feelings of her heart. I borrow'd Lindsay's name, not in the hope I cou'd impose on your sagacity, but as a cover only for the moment, till I cou'd find how her affections stood, and where they pointed.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Stop there, and tell me whether those supplies, which have subsisted her, were your's or not.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: All mine, and Varnish is dismiss'd for ever.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: There, there! I said it. Now my word comes true. Varnish has kick'd me out of his employ. Now I'll take in his bill, return his visit, and civilly congratulate him on his disgrace.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: 'Tis dangerous playing with edg'd-tools, my friend. Take care of Varnish. Above all, remember that I am Lindsay still; there yet remains one conference more with Julia, 'ere I drop the mask, and resume my proper person. Will you consent to this, and keep the secret?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Yes, and because my Dolly bears me out that you are no apothecary, I'll go and swear you are the very best that ever grasp'd a pestle.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Come, my dear Julia, lay aside reserve. Let me have no apologies. My time is perfectly at your command: My heart is warmly interested in your happiness, and to render you any service wou'd afford me the sincerest pleasure.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Ah, that is kind indeed! I feel your goodness; but as you cannot mitigate my sorrows, why shou'd I trouble you with the recital of them?

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: I can condole with you at least, and that is in some slight degree a comfort.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: My story is soon told. My dying father bequeathed me to the protection of Captain Sentamour—Nay more, he breath'd his life out in a prayer, that Providence wou'd so dispose our fate, as might unite us heart and hand for life.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Well! what prevents it?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: On the part of Sentamour nothing has been omitted. I have subsisted, and do still subsist, upon his bounty—But I never saw him—

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: And you have seen Lindsay—Is it not so?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Yes, it is so.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Well! Lindsay is the friend of Sentamour, his advocate; and pleads so movingly, that your soft heart is melted by his suit—Am I not right?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Oh yes, you are very right.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: And you are very much in love, my dear, or I am very wrong.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Ah now, don't say so. What a shocking creature must I appear to you, if that were true!

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Unfortunate perhaps, not shocking.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Ingrateful, base, unnatural!—What right have I, who live upon the bounty of Sentamour, to think of any else? What wou'd my father say, were he alive?

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Love little cares what living fathers say, or dead one's dictate in their parting hours. Love turns the benefactor from the door, and lets in the betrayer: so high Love holds his own supremacy, that he makes every passion own his powers.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Heavens! what a horrid picture do you paint of my incurable and desperate casè!

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: No, no, your case is not quite desperate. Love, like the viper, carries its own cure. Time will draw out the venom from your wound; but 'tis a tedious process. There is a quicker remedy in your reach.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Aye! what is that?

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Marriage—an authoriz'd and sovereign remedy—all other practice is but quackery and dangerous dabbling with the constitution.
Well! why do you come here? what do you want with me?

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Nay, I don't know. I come here I believe only because I can't help it.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Who is this gentleman?

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Mr. Lindsay, a particular friend of mine. Give me leave to present him to you.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: You have been out of England some time, Mr. Lindsay.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Some years, Madam.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: And with Captain Sentamour all the time?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: We have never been separated.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: So I understand from Mandeville— and is the Captain coming to Bath?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Not coming.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Humph!—I understand he has been very successful.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: He has avail'd himself of some lucky opportunities.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: And some that might be lucky, I perceive, he overlooks. He may have taken prizes enough to make his fortune; there is yet one wanting to complete his happiness.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: I am perfectly of your opinion, Madam.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: I perfectly believe you. Nobody can live in the near contemplation of such charms, and be insensible to their influence.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Mandeville, for heaven's sake bring me off.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Come, Louisa, you must release this lady and gentleman: I believe they are engag'd.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: And so agreeably engag'd, it would be cruel to detain them. Adieu, my dear Julia, a good walk to you: shall I wait upon you down the stairs?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Oh, by no means. Mr. Lindsay will take care of me.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: “Mr. Lindsay will take care of me!”—Yes, excellent care—such care as a hawk takes of a dove, or an alderman of a turtle. Lord help us, us poor women out of love, say I! Soft, simple, silly souls as we are, it makes dreadful havoc with our slender wits.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Ah Louisa, Louisa! I doubt much if it will ever get into your heart, or mount up to your head. O' my conscience I believe you know no more of love than I do of the Sanchrite language.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: How should I, when nobody is at the pains to teach me, and I can't acquire it by inspiration? I have been flatter'd by the men— that is not love: envied and abused by the women—that is not flattery. I should laugh at the coxcomb, who prais'd my beauty; I should despise the booby, who complimented me for my wit. I would be treated by the world as if I had common sense; nobody does that, therefore I treat every body as they treat me; and because I generally find fair appearances to be false upon trial, I get the character of a jilt and a coquette—but this is an old story, and I am tir'd of it. I'll sing you a Song.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Let me prevail with you this once to have patience to listen to me, and charity not to laugh at me. I would fain say a few words to you just now about a poor awkward honest fellow of your acquaintance—

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Meaning yourself—say on!

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: I shall make a blundering business of it, for I am not eloquent, and if once you put me down, there's an end of me. I shall never rally.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Well; anything to accommodate you.—Let me see. Can't I contrive to carry on a discourse with you, and not speak a word?

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: How can that be done?

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: For instance—When you put a question, or advance a sentiment, and I nod, it means yes—

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Very good.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: When I shake my head, it means no.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Yes; but nothing is so ugly as a shaking head.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Well then, when I do neither one nor the other, it means nothing.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Agreed! and now to put your tokens to the test—Louisa, charming, captivating Louisa! Do you not perceive I am irrecoverably in love with you?
Very good; that means, yes. You have found out I am in love with you. Once more—Hav'nt you found out also I am a very silly fellow for my pains?
—Better still; that means, no. I am not a silly fellow for being in love with you—Then what prevents me from proposing to you?
—Why that is best of all, for that means nothing. Nothing prevents my absolutely proposing. Now then for the important, the conclusive question— If I propose, will you consent? Death to my hopes!
—You will not consent. Have you no pity for the man that loves you? Have you so long known me, Louisa, and can you now renounce me?

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Can I renounce the world, and its allurements? that is the question.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: No, no; renounce it! Live, and be still its grace and ornament.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: That is a lover's, not a husband's speech. I must dismiss my follies, and be wise. How long do you think t'will take to work that change? At least a twelvemonth?

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: I shan't live out half the time.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: What are you talking of? You won't live out half the day, for Varnish swears vengeance against you for driving him out of Julia Clareville's good graces, only because you want to gain her to yourself.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: That is a gross falsehood, and I can give proof positive to the contrary.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: What proof? Assertions are no proofs. Words will not pass. Every body believes he is making court to Julia: The whole place has it that you have positively refus'd him.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: The whole place is mistaken: I have done no such thing; and you may tell that fellow Varnish, if he dares to propagate such calumnies against me, I will confute him, and bring him to public shame, by marrying Mandeville to-morrow.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: There, there, John Mandeville, do you hear that? If you don't run mad for joy, it can only be, because you have no senses to lose.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Hold! not so fast. Don't start false premises and then draw rash conclusions. You have trap'd me into a sort of a promise, which I am neither equitably bound to fulfil, nor spitefully determined to revoke. In the first place Mandeville is to wait a whole twelve-month, till I am completely metamorphos'd into a good kind of body, and thoroughly reconcil'd to live in his execrable old castle in Glamorganshire—That will take six months at least.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: I'll pull it down, and build a new one in half the time.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: No, you must not touch it. I shall be very fond of it when I have got other castles out of my head. I must have six months more to learn all the elegant and ornamental arts.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: You have them all: You possess every one of them You are elegance itself.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Not a grain of it. I know nothing of the elegant œconomy of a chicken-yard or a dairy: of the ornamental art of making pyes and puddings I am profoundly ignorant. I have not yet familiariz'd myself to the pleasant odour of tobacco, and not a single move at backgammon do I know, so help me truth.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Pooh, pooh, Louisa, now you are turning every thing to joke and ridicule.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: It is no joke let me tell you. What am I to do with the Parson? How am I to entertain the Exciseman, and recommend myself to the Natives? All these things, and a hundred others, not forgetting my abhorrence of Welch ale and toasted cheese, can't be got over in less than a twelvemonth—Can they, uncle?

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: In something less, according to my calculation?

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: What is your calculation?

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Come home with me, Louisa, and I will shew it you delineated to the life.
