In the fore-ground there is an honest virtuous husband—In the middle space a smiling scene of peace and plenty—And, in the back ground, an enchanting groupe of blooming cherubs, your posterity, in long and indeterminate perspective.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: A family-piece I perceive.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: It is a family piece, and you must beware how you look at it with an eye of ridicule; for that, like the camera obscura, turns every thing upside down.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Never fear; we will be very serious. Mandeville, this family-piece will be a most valuable ornament to your old castle. You must take care to hang it in a good light.

div.stage: Enter Varnish, followed by a Servant.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Mr. Hartshorn the apothecary is waiting, Sir, and desires to speak with you.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: What does he want with me? Bid him leave his bill, and be gone; I have nothing more to do with him—Stop! where are you going? Tell him to come up.
He must have some commission for this visit—some overture perhaps from Julia Clareville, who may have seen her folly and repented.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Humble servant, Mr. Varnish.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Your most obedient, Mr. Hartshorn? To what happy chance am I indebted for the honor of this visit?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: I understand you call'd at my house when I was from home. Having ceas'd my visits to you as a patient, I did not quite expect you would return them to me as an apothecary. Beg to know your commands.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: None for you Mr. Hartshorn, none in life. Your door stood open, and I turned into your house.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: There are many gentlemen welcome to turn into my house, as often they see fit: there are others in the world as welcome to turn out of it.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: I understand you, Sir. All dealings between you and me are at an end.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Entirely, and I flatter myself I can say you are the first living patient that ever put me out of your employ. Some indeed have taken leave of me for a very natural reason, and the rest have still a kindness for the Golden Mortar. I had the honor of being of some service to you, and carrying you through a dangerous attack. I never charg'd you even the fraction of a pill or potion, that I did not send in, trusting it might do you good, if you took it and very sure it could not do you harm if you did not take it.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: I have no fault to find with you as an apothecary. It is when you step out of that character, and instil evil thoughts of me into Julia Clareville, that I have just reason to complain of you, and consider your interference as officious and impertinent.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Call it what you will, you can't deny that it was honest.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: And if you had not been what you are, when I overheard you warning her against me, I should have treated you as you deserve.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Treat every man as he deserves, and what would have been your situation, when you was detected in taking credit for benefactions you never had bestow'd?

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Intolerable insolence! must I bear such language from an apothecary?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Can you justify such conduct as a gentleman? If you had kept to your character, I had not gone out of mine. If you had been as careful of your honor, as I have been of your health, you wou'd never have heard this language from an apothecary.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Who waits?—
Turn that insolent fellow out of my doors

sp.speaker: Hart.
sp.p: Have a care, friend, what you do. I don't mean to be turn'd out either by you or your master. If you attempt to lay hands upon me, I shall lay my cane upon you, and probably make a worse crack in your scull than I shall be able to cure,
There, Sir, your servant prudently declines the attempt; will you be pleas'd to undertake it yourself?

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: No, Sir; if I must be concern'd with the firm of the Golden Mortar, I shall take out your partner Lindsay, who has at least the appearance of a gentleman, and treat you, as I ever have done, with indifference and contempt. Now will you be pleas'd to walk quietly out of my house?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: As quietly as you can desire; only remember, Mr. Varnish, that a man, who has fac'd the perils of the sea, and the cannon of the enemy, is not to be frighted by a few windy words; for tho' I put a Mortar on my door, with Surgeon, Apothecary, and Man-midwife under it, I write Gentleman over all, and will not be treated with contempt. So, now I am off, and that you may know where to find me, here's my bill—Pay it at your leisure.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Insolent savage! Take up his dirty bill, and follow me.

sp.speaker: Sir Mathew.
sp.p: Raven, I am going to talk to you more like a friend than a master.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: I'm glad of it. I hope it won't be all talk, and nothing else.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: I am this day made the happiest fellow in existence. Mandeville is to be married to Louisa Davenant.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: And why does that make you so happy?

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Because if he had not taken a wife, I must.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: You have had an escape.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: I have been making my will, and settling my estate.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Very proper. He may have heirs and keep it in the family.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: And because you are an idle, good- for-nothing scape-grace, whom I have spoil'd, and nobody after me will endure, I have hook'd you into a small nook of my will, and left you a wherewithal when I am gone.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: Aye, Sir; when you are gone, Heaven knows I shall want a wherewithal to comfort me; but pray don't be in any hurry to go on my account; and above all, don't stint yourself in your legacy, as supposing I have sav'd any money in your service. No, Sir, I have copied your example in most things. You liv'd well, and spent your income; so did I, and spent my earnings. You lov'd wine and women; I had no dislike to either. You was a little given to quarelling, turn'd out in three duels, and was whip't thro' the small guts in the last; I fought my way thro' the whole Free and Easy Club, and was kick'd down stairs with two broken ribs at the concluding battle.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Reprobate! Don't boast of your enormities, and then say you copied them from me.

sp.speaker: Rav.
sp.p: I wish I had copied you a little closer; you have liv'd single; I married.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Well, Sirrah, I am going to reform; copy me in that. I shall pass the remainder of my days with my nephew John in Glamorganshire, repose myself in the venerable mansion of my ancestors, lead a quiet moral life, and emulate the simplicity of their manners. Leave me.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Ah my dear uncle, it is all over with me if you don't stand my friend. This man will hear no reason. I have abated him eleven months out of the twelve, and now he wants me to give up the poor little honey moon, which I have reserv'd to myself before marriage, as a qualifier for all the vinegar moons that will follow after it:—Is that fair?

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Perfectly otherwise, and I advise you not to give up an atom of your right, unless you are disposed to do it as your own free gift.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: I don't believe I shall be so dispos'd, but I won't be positive, and put him out of all hope. I'll consider of it.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Do so, my dear; 'tis as much as he can expect.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: He knows how I hate noise and bustle, and a fuss about things of small consequence; therefore I bar all bell-ringers, bawling flower-women, city music, and the intolerable din of marrow-bones and cleavers: I denounce all white cockades, wedding favours, and surfeiting plumb-cake: If he ventures to present himself to me upon the fatal day in a new glossy suit of bottle-green, and a staring tuft of hair, cockatoo fashion, on the crown of his head, I'll swear the peace against him— but if all things are done silently and quietly, then perhaps—

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: What then?

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Why then perhaps they can't be done too quickly—So here's my hand in pledge of faith, in token of affection. From this moment, Mandeville, I am your's for life; on you I will depend. When the church has join'd us, let the chaise take us off, and the castle take us in.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: Oh! my soul's better part; my joy, my blessing!—

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Hold, hold, hold! No raptures, if you please. Order yourself quietly, and give me no fine names till I have deserved them.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Mr. Varnish desires leave to speak with you in private.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Let Varnish have his conference, and we will take our walk. I have promis'd myself to poor lovesick Julia, and have Mandeville's permission to impart to her a secret, on the discovery of which her happiness depends.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Tell Mr. Varnish I am at his service.
This coxcomb either has some project in his head, or some quarrel on his hands, I am ill disposed to help him on with either.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Sir Mathew Moribund, I resort to you as to a gentleman, whose friendship I have long experienc'd, and whose courage no man ever doubted. I am just now in that predicament, in which you, Sir, more than once have found yourself, and applied no doubt to your friends for assistance, as I am now compelled to do to mine.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: An affair of honour, I presume; in plainer words—a duel.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Precisely that.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: I'm sorry for it.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: With an obscure fellow, I confess— by profession, a surgeon—by name, Lindsay— I have call'd him out to atone for his scurrility; he has promis'd himself to the meeting. It is now drawing near to the hour, and I am unprovided with a second.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Perhaps you look to me for that office.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: To whom can I so worthily entrust my honour and my life?

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: I must absolutely decline it. I am past the age of chivalry. One mistake I lose no time to set you right in:—The gentleman you conceive to be a surgeon, and describe as an obscure fellow, is an officer high in character; his name is not Lindsay; it is Sentamour.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Sir, are you sure of this?

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: There is no doubt; and whatever may have been his reasons hitherto for concealing himself, I am persuaded he will not meet you under any other name or character than his true one. Now, Sir, let me counsel you to recollect yourself in time, and in that case, if you will accept of me as your mediator, a mutual explanation may do every thing away, and I will most readily undertake it.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Sir Mathew, I comprehend both the letter and the spirit of your proposal. The letter, give me leave to say, does not exactly apply to my case; and the spirit, under favour, does by no means meet my expectations. I have the honour to wish you a good day.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Who waits? Attend upon Mr. Varnish.

div.head: SCENE II.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: 'Tis not a pleasant business, Lindsay, I must own; but there is no avoiding it; say no more upon the subject. We are a little before our time. Who is this that follows us?
—Hartshorn, what brings you hither?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Give me time to fetch my breath. 'Sdeath, Sir, I have burst the very braces of my heart, and carried away all my running tackle in chase of you.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: And now you have found me, what is your business with me?

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: What is my business with you? Duty. What is your's with Varnish? Danger. Here are the instruments to save your life; these are the weapons to revenge your death.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: No, no; take notice, I declare against revenge. I am provided with a second. This gentleman is my friend.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: It's very well; it's mighty well. I mean the gentleman no offence, but I must say, Captain Sentamour, I think it rather hard in you to overlook a poor old seaman, who would die a thousand deaths for you, and take a youngster for your second, who can die but once, and perhaps had rather not die at all.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: You ought to know him, and I ought to introduce him to you as Mr. Lindsay; but this is no time for that, especially as I perceive Mr. Varnish is approaching.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Captain Sentamour, I presume.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: At your service. You are alone, Sir.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: I am, as you see, unprovided with a second. The time was short, and I have been disappointed in my application.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Use your pleasure, Mr. Varnish. Appoint another time; and if your anger cools, I shan't be sorry.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: This gentleman, I conclude, is your second. Mr. Hartshorn, I take for granted, attends in his professional capacity. I am in your hands, Captain Sentamour; but I dare say I may rely upon your honour in every possible event.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: You will make your option. I repeat my offer; and you will either adjourn our meeting till you are better provided, or come to an explanation on the spot, as you see fit. Gentlemen, be pleased to step aside, and withdraw yourselves out of hearing.

Mr. Varnish, as I now present myself to you by a different name and character from what I fictitiously assumed at our first meeting, I hold myself bound so far to atone to you for the deception, as to assure you, I can retain no resentment as Captain Sentamour for any expressions you made use of towards me as Mr. Lindsay. I beg therefore to be understood, that, although I meet you in this place, I have no quarrel with you, no desire to attempt your life, nor any wish to risk my own.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Captain Sentamour, I nourish no particular inveteracy against you in my heart, but I have always conducted myself according to the rules of honour; and I know not how they can well be dispensed with on this occasion.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: If you have positively made your decision, Sir, you can't proceed too quickly; for the longer time you give yourself for reflecting upon sanguinary meas ues, the less will be your chance for exculpation, when you are brought to an account for them. As for me, Mr. Varnish, belonging as I do to another service, I confess I have ever held it as a matter of duty to avoid all private quarrels. To my Country I have pledg'd my life; and, if you did the same, your courage wou'd be well applied, for believe me she has need of every one of us.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Yes, and your public services have made your honour safe; I perhaps, have not the same resource. You have secur'd the good opinion of the world; I have to guard myself against it's censure and contempt.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Granted. I have exonerated my conscience. I tender you perfect reconciliation, and engage, if you agree to it, to guarantee your honour. You are here alone; refer yourself to your friends, and consult their judgment on the case. You hardly will object to that proposal.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: No, Sir, I do not object to that proposal, neither can I scruple to leave my honour in your hands, when you engage to guarantee it. I now perceive, Captain Sentamour, that true courage cannot consist in my past notions of false honour. I thank you for the lesson you have given me: There are few men living, perhaps, from whom I wou'd have taken it; and now to make the best atonement in my power to Miss Julia Clareville, I will instantly take my departure from Bath; and, as the strongest proof I can give you of a perfect reconciliation, here is my hand, sincerely tender'd; and with it a wish, not less sincere, that you may be happy in the possession of the most amiable woman in existence.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Stop, if you please. Your motives for leaving Bath, as far as they respect Miss Clareville, I perfectly understand. They do honour to your sensibility; but as the guardian of your reputation in this affair, which we have now dismiss'd, I must advise you to revoke your purpose; as, by staying with us sometime longer, you will make that clear to all the world, which a hasty departure might leave doubtful, and subject to malicious misinterpretation. Am I not right?

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: You are perfectly right, and I am oblig'd to you for the advice.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Let us then walk home together, and, with your permission, we will take my friends with us by the way.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: With all my heart.

Alas! Alas! how my sad heart is tortur'd with distracting thoughts! Lindsay must be insensible and blind, if he does not discover how I love him. He does, he does, and cruelly contrives to bind those fetters every moment faster, from which he should assist me to break loose. I must, I will exert one timely effort, or I am lost for ever!

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Julia, my dear, I bring you a proposal, which you must positively not refuse me. Nay, don't put on that grave discouraging face. It offers pleasure to you, my sweet girl, because it calls you to an entertainment, where all are friends; and Lindsay will be present.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Ah, Madam! were I not the weakest wretch that ever doated on her own destruction, Lindsay's the very man I should avoid.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: That would be mere coquetry, my dear; you must perceive that he's in love with you.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: With me?

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: With you.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Impossible!

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Decidedly; desperately—with whom else do you suppose him to be in love? With dame Hartshorn? With the dirty drug shop? Which is it, think you, your pretty face, or the golden gallipot over your door, that allures him to play the part of the apothecary, when all the while his real cast is that of Romeo, the god of your idolatry?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: What do you mean? You puzzle me, my dearest madam, you bewilder me: I am giddy with conjecture. Is he, or is he not, the man he passes for?

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: The man he passes for! No, surely; he would pass on nobody for an apothecary, that was not in want of hellebore and a strait waistcoat. Open your eyes, unless love has blinded them; and the next time you see Lindsay, you will discover Sentamour.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Oh! my dear madam, tell me, tell me truly. May I believe it? Are you well informed?

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: Here's my informer. Mandeville will tell you.

sp.speaker: Mand.
sp.p: You speak of Sentamour. The secret's out. He no longer wishes to disguise himself. I met him in full uniform with Lindsay not long ago. I think he'll soon be here.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Heaven grant he may!

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: My visit is to Captain Sentamour. Who can direct me to him?

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Aye, who indeed? You, Sir, perhaps can tell me if Varnish has not challeng'd him to fight.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: I wish that I could tell you he has not.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: There, there! I am the fatal cause. Unhappy Sentamour! for me he bleeds!

div.stage: Sentamour enters, and runs to Julia.

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Julia, my beloved Julia! I now address you in my real character; and if, as Lindsay, I have happily gain'd an interest in your heart, I hope I shall not forfeit it, as Sentamour, the friend of your father, honour'd by his approbation, and in his latest moments recommended to your choice.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: How happy I must be to find the friend of my father, and the man of my heart, one and the same person, may be conceived, but cannot be express'd. Captain Sentamour will draw his conclusions, and spare me the confusion of a more explicit declaration.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Here, here! come the rest of the parties.

Varnish, give me your hand; this is as it should be. Now we meet in peace to shut the temple of Janus, and stick the olive branch in the Golden Mortar over the door of it.— Hartshorn, my dear fellow, though I wish you all possible good luck in your vocation, I am glad to see these gentlemen have cut you out no custom.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: Thank the fates, brother Lindsay, we have no surgeon's work on this occasion. I had better have been your patient, than Sentamour's should have been mine; for tho' there is no scarcity of brave officers in our Navy, there is a lumping overplus of apothecaries, and I should not have been miss'd amongst the number.

sp.speaker: Varn.
sp.p: Captain Sentamour, have I your permission to address a few words to that much injured lady, and humbly intercede for pardon?— Miss Clareville, I am too deeply sensible of my errors to attempt any defence of them. The only claim I can make to your forgiveness, is, that being now convinc'd I did not deserve you, and that Captain Sentamour does, I am thoroughly asham'd of the unfair means I took to mislead your attention, and beg leave to congratulate you on the happy choice you have made.

sp.speaker: Julia.
sp.p: Ah, now, Mr. Varnish, this is all too much, for any thing you may think I had occasion to resent. Believe me, Sir, when you are pleas'd to charge yourself, you for ever do away all remembrance of offence, and leave me only sensible to your candour and condescension.

sp.speaker: Sir Math.
sp.p: Come, my good friends, we have happily dismiss'd the business of this day: Tomorrow business of a better sort auspiciously awaits us. Let us devote some portion of the interval to good fellowship, and join our wishes for a happy union of devoted hearts. How stand your inclinations, gallant Sir, to this proposal?

sp.speaker: Sent.
sp.p: Most cordially I close with it; and if my charming Julia will consider how precious to a Seaman every moment is, that duty spares him to devote to love, she will consent to let tomorrow be alike auspicious to me as to my friend.

sp.speaker: Louisa.
sp.p: I hope you don't expect an answer. Her silence and her blushes speak consent. Trust me for deciding upon symptoms.

sp.speaker: Harts.
sp.p: I hope that I can give some little guess at symptoms also. Therefore, if YOU, my Patients and kind Customers this night will but bestow some token of your favour, and dismiss your humble servant to my bed in peace, I will recruit my spirits for to-morrow, and with your permission inscribe upon my labels, in the true style of the shop—The same to be repeated.
